title: Mon chat peut ? · Can my cat eat this? Answers in 3 seconds
description: Type any food: the Mon chat peut ? app tells you in 3 seconds whether your cat can eat it, why, and how much. Meal plans and weight tracking included.
og_desc: Type any food: the app tells you in 3 seconds whether your cat can eat it, why, and how much.
og_alt: Can my cat eat chocolate? No! Vivi, the app's cat, sulks.
nav_top_label: Mon chat peut ?, back to top
h1: Mon chat peut ? Find out in 3 seconds whether your cat can eat a food, and why.
reason_init: Chocolate contains theobromine and caffeine, which cats get rid of very poorly.
picks_label: Type a food into the sentence, or try:
count_init: Demo with {n} foods. The app also recognizes dishes from a photo and reads barcodes.
moment_alt: Seen from the table: a fork holds a piece of salmon, and Vivi stares at it over the edge of the table.
moment_title: Your cat is staring. You're holding the fork.
moment_lede: So you google “can my cat eat tuna”. Ten tabs later, here's what you've got:
snip1: Tuna is their favorite, go for it!
snip2: NEVER give tuna, it's full of mercury.
snip3: A little is fine, just not in oil. Or maybe it is?
snip4: Mine has eaten it every day for 15 years.
answer_text: A bit of plain tuna now and then is fine. Every day, no: too much mercury, and a risk of vitamin E deficiency.
day_lede: Vivi is on a diet. Scroll through her day: the app is there from the first meal to the bedtime read.
ds_verdict_text: Mafé: onion and garlic are toxic.
ds_adjust: Plan adjusted: −3% calories, due to weight gain.
read_body: Hydration is key to your cat's kidney and urinary health. Here's how to spot the good signs.
step1_text: Age, weight, goal: the app works out her portion. For Vivi, 44 g of kibble and 176 kcal a day.
step2_text: You snap a photo of your mafé. The AI spots peanut, onion and garlic, and answers: no.
step3_text: You log her meals and her weight. Vivi gained 100 g: the plan adjusts on its own, −3% calories.
step4_text: Hydration, kibble, ideal weight: 4-minute guides, written simply.
step5_text: Her weight curve and the protein, fat and carb split. Vivi lost 500 g in 8 weeks.
founder_title: I built this app for my own cats.
founder_text: Every evening, the same question over my plate. Online lists contradicted each other, and forums even more so. I wanted a clear answer, with the reason and the right amount, in a few seconds. Then a plan to keep them in shape.
faq1_a: No. The app helps with everyday decisions. If your cat has swallowed something toxic, call your vet or an animal poison control center right away, without waiting for symptoms.
faq2_q: How does the app recognize a dish?
faq2_a: Take a photo or type its name. The AI identifies the food and its likely ingredients (onion, garlic, salt…), then gives you the verdict with an explanation.
faq3_q: I have several cats. Does it work?
faq3_a: Yes. Each cat has its own profile: age, weight, goal, meal plan and tracking. Switch between them in one tap.
faq4_a: Not yet. The app is available on Android, and the iPhone version is coming soon.
faq5_a: We only collect what the app needs. You can view, correct or delete your account and your cats' data at any time (GDPR).
final_title: Next time your cat stares at you during dinner, you'll know.
final_fine: Available on Android. The iPhone version is coming soon.

foods: Chocolate contains theobromine and caffeine, which cats get rid of very poorly. Even a single square can cause vomiting, tremors and heart rhythm problems. The darker it is, the more dangerous.
Raw, cooked or powdered, onion damages a cat's red blood cells and can cause anemia. Watch out for sauces, soups and ready meals that contain it.
Same family as onion, but more concentrated. Garlic attacks red blood cells, and the effects can take several days to show.
Like onion and garlic, it's an allium. Raw or cooked, it's toxic to a cat's red blood cells.
Grapes are linked to serious kidney damage in dogs, and no one knows the dangerous dose. To be safe, never give a cat grapes or raisins.
Mafé usually contains fatty peanut paste, and often onions, garlic and spices. Onion and garlic are toxic to cats, and fatty or salty dishes can cause vomiting, diarrhea or pancreatitis.
Zucchini isn't toxic to cats and can be given in small amounts, raw or cooked. It has few of the nutrients a cat needs, so keep it occasional.
A bit of plain tuna now and then is fine. Every day, no: too much mercury, and a risk of vitamin E deficiency. Avoid tuna in oil or brine.
Most adult cats digest lactose poorly: bloating and diarrhea. If you want to treat them, there is lactose-free cat milk.
A small cube of hard cheese is usually fine, since it has little lactose. But it's fatty and salty: a rare treat, not a habit.
A little plain, unsweetened yogurt is often well tolerated. Never fruit yogurt, and never with sweeteners.
Cooked chicken is an excellent source of protein. Skinless, boneless and unseasoned: no salt, no garlic, no onion.
Cooked, plain and boneless, turkey is a lean protein cats love. Skip turkey deli meat, which is too salty.
Plain cooked beef is perfect. Cook it through, with no seasoning.
Not toxic, but very salty and often full of preservatives. A small piece once in a while, no more.
Too fatty, too salty, and often seasoned with garlic. Keep it for yourself.
Cooked, boneless and unseasoned, salmon provides protein and omega-3s. Avoid smoked salmon, which is far too salty.
Far too salty for a cat. Go for a piece of plain cooked salmon instead.
Raw fish contains an enzyme that destroys vitamin B1 and can carry parasites. Cooked is better.
In water, with no added salt: a good treat now and then. Avoid sardines in oil or tomato sauce.
Cooked, peeled and plain, shrimp is a much-loved treat. No raw shrimp, and nothing in sauce.
A cooked egg, hard-boiled or scrambled without salt or butter, provides good protein. Never raw: risk of salmonella.
raw egg|raw eggs|raw egg yolk|raw egg white
Risk of salmonella, and raw egg white blocks the absorption of a vitamin (biotin). Always cooked.
Cooked bones splinter into shards that can injure the mouth, esophagus or gut.
Very rich in vitamin A. A little now and then is good. Too often, it can cause vitamin A toxicity.
Plain cooked rice is easy to digest and helps with minor tummy trouble. It gives a cat almost nothing, so only as a side.
Cooked and plain, it's not dangerous, but useless for a carnivore. Never with garlic or onion sauce.
A small piece of baked bread is no problem, but adds nothing. Raw dough, on the other hand, is dangerous: it ferments in the stomach.
Raw dough swells and ferments in the stomach, producing alcohol. It's a vet emergency.
Cooked and cut small, carrot goes down well. Raw, it's hard to chew.
Low in calories and full of water, cucumber is safe in small pieces.
Boiled and unsalted, they can even help a cat on a diet feel full.
Cooked and plain, pumpkin brings fiber that helps digestion. A teaspoon is enough.
Cooked peas are safe. You'll even find them in some kibble.
Steamed and in small amounts, broccoli is safe.
Not toxic, but rich in oxalates. Avoid it completely if your cat has urinary or kidney problems.
The flesh of a ripe tomato is fine in small amounts. The leaves, stems and green tomatoes contain solanine: toxic.
Cooked and plain, in small amounts: OK. Raw or green, never, it contains solanine. Fries, too fatty and salty, are out as well.
Very fatty, and the pit, skin and leaves contain persin. Best avoided entirely.
A few small pieces, peeled, without core or seeds. The seeds contain cyanogenic compounds.
Not toxic, but very sugary. One slice now and then, no more.
Lots of cats love melon. A few small cubes without the rind are OK, but it's sugary.
Seedless and without the rind, a few small cubes are refreshing. It's still sugar.
Not toxic. A few pieces once in a while, no more.
Safe in small amounts. A few berries are plenty.
Citrus fruits contain citric acid and essential oils that irritate the digestive system. Most cats hate the smell, and that's a good thing.
The pits, stems and leaves contain cyanogenic compounds, and a swallowed pit can block the gut.
Very fatty and hard to digest, and some, like macadamia, are toxic to dogs. No nuts.
Not toxic in themselves, but very fatty, often salted, and some peanut butters contain xylitol. Best avoided.
Caffeine is toxic to cats: agitation, racing heart, tremors. Watch out for coffee grounds and pods too.
Even a small amount of alcohol can be serious for a cat. Watch out for boozy desserts too.
Not a food, but the question comes up often: lilies are deadly to cats. A chewed leaf or pollen licked off the fur can cause acute kidney failure.
That's what it's for. They can chew it, sniff it and roll in it.
Not toxic, but not suitable: it lacks taurine, which cats need. Once by mistake is no problem.
Lactose and sugar: a bad combination. Some ice creams also contain chocolate or xylitol.
Dough, fatty cheese, sauce with garlic and onion, cured meat: pretty much everything you shouldn't.
Cooked and plain, safe in small amounts. Never the cob, which can block the gut.
A drop in the bowl is no problem. Too much, and it's diarrhea.
Often sweetened with xylitol, and a choking hazard. Keep it out of reach.
Store-bought button mushrooms, cooked and plain, are fine in small amounts. Wild mushrooms, never.
